draft.title: Drafting and editing
card: getting your ideas down in full, without stopping to fix them. A first draft can be rough.
changing the structure and meaning of the piece. You might move a paragraph, add a missing idea or cut a part that does not fit.
fixing sentences and words. You correct spelling, punctuation and grammar, and choose sharper words.
Strong writers also cut words that add nothing. In "She quickly ran very fast", quickly and very fast repeat what ran already suggests.
draft.remember: Draft to get ideas down, revise to change the big picture, edit to fix the small details.

a.q: Which task is an example of revising, not editing?
opts: Moving the strongest scene from the middle to the opening
Fixing a missing comma in the second paragraph
Swapping a vague verb for a more exact one
Correcting the spelling of a character's name
a.why: Moving a scene changes the structure of the piece, so it is revising. The other three fix sentences or words, which is editing. Swapping a verb can seem big, but it is a change to a single word.
a.clue: Revising changes the shape of the whole piece.

b.q: Leo's story draft has a stronger idea at the end than at the start. He moves it to the opening, then trims "very, very tired" to "exhausted". Which describes his two changes, in order?
b.why: Moving the idea changes the structure of the piece, so it is revising. Trimming "very, very tired" to one exact word fixes the wording and cuts words that add nothing, so it is editing. Neither change is drafting, because the ideas are already down.
b.clue: One change moves a big part. The other fixes the wording.

a.best: Moving the strongest scene from the middle to the opening
